title: Learning Checks
description: Starter tests you can replace with your own JSON file. They also show the optional learning fields: answer keys, a one-line why, misconception notes for wrong options, a hint ladder, rubrics, and prerequisites.

tests.title: Web Fundamentals
tests.relevance: These come up in almost every front-end interview, and they decide whether a page is accessible, adapts to any screen, and stays snappy under load.
tests.instructions: Answer from memory. Use examples when they help.

questions.prompt: What problem does semantic HTML solve?
questions.expectedAnswer: Semantic HTML gives content meaning so browsers, assistive technology, and search engines can understand its structure.
questions.why: A <nav> or <button> carries meaning a <div> doesn't — screen readers, keyboard navigation, and search all rely on it.

questions.prompt: Which CSS layout tool is best for two-dimensional page layouts?
questions.why: Grid controls rows and columns at the same time; Flexbox lays things out along one axis.

misconceptions.Flexbox: Flexbox is one-dimensional — great for a row or a column, awkward for both at once.
misconceptions.Float: Floats were a workaround for wrapping text around images, not a layout system.
misconceptions.Position absolute: Absolute positioning takes elements out of the flow, so nothing responds to their size.

questions.prompt: await pauses the whole JavaScript thread until the promise settles.
questions.why: await only suspends the current async function; the event loop keeps running other work.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript.
questions.expectedAnswer: Synchronous code runs line by line and blocks until each step finishes. Asynchronous code starts an operation, such as a network request or timer, and continues; the result is handled later through callbacks, promises, or async/await when the event loop picks it up.
rubric: Says synchronous code blocks until each step finishes
Says asynchronous work continues without waiting
Mentions the event loop or callback queue
Gives a concrete example such as fetch or setTimeout
hints: Think about what happens to the next line while a network request is in flight.
Something has to decide when a finished request's callback actually runs.

tests.title: Git Basics
tests.relevance: Clean commits and safe review habits are what teammates notice first.

questions.prompt: What does staging a file mean in Git?
questions.expectedAnswer: Staging adds the file's current changes to the index so they are included in the next commit.
questions.why: The staging area lets you choose exactly which changes go into a commit, instead of everything in the working tree.

questions.prompt: Which commands show changes before you commit? Select all that apply.
questions.why: diff shows unstaged edits, diff --staged shows what will be committed, and status lists which files changed.

misconceptions.git push: push sends commits that already exist — by then it's too late to review them locally.
misconceptions.git reset --hard: reset --hard throws changes away; it doesn't show them.

questions.prompt: Describe a safe workflow for reviewing changes before committing.
rubric: Checks git status to see which files changed
Reviews unstaged changes with git diff
Stages deliberately (git add -p or specific files)
Reviews staged changes with git diff --staged before committing

tests.title: Git Collaboration
tests.relevance: Builds on Git Basics: once your own commits are clean, the next skill is sharing them safely.

questions.prompt: You pushed a branch that others have pulled. What's the safe way to undo a bad commit on it?
options: Delete the branch and recreate it
questions.why: revert adds a new commit that undoes the change, so nobody else's history is rewritten.

misconceptions.git reset --hard HEAD~1 then force-push: Rewriting shared history breaks everyone who already pulled it.
misconceptions.git commit --amend then force-push: Amending also rewrites the commit — same problem as reset on a shared branch.

questions.prompt: What does git fetch do that git pull doesn't?
questions.expectedAnswer: git fetch downloads remote commits without merging them into your branch, so you can inspect them first.
questions.why: pull is fetch plus merge (or rebase); fetch alone never changes your working branch.
